chapters.title: Chapter 4: Beyond Percentages: Control, Rights and Exits

lessons.title: Liquidation Preference: Why Founders Can Get Less Than Their Percentage at Exit

children.text: An acquirer offers ₹60 crore for TiffinBox. Meera and Rohan hold 28.51% of the company between them, so they do the obvious sum and expect about ₹17 crore. What they actually receive is ₹6.08 crore. Nothing has gone wrong, nobody has cheated them, and every rupee of the difference was agreed in term sheets they signed years earlier. This is the liquidation preference at work.

body.text: Your ownership percentage tells you how the money is split after the investors have been paid what they are owed. Below a certain exit price, founders own a large share of nothing.

markDefs.definition: A contractual right for preference shareholders to be paid a defined amount out of exit proceeds before ordinary shareholders receive anything.

children.text: Indian venture investors almost always hold compulsorily convertible preference shares, and those shares carry a

. In plain terms: on a sale of the company, the investor gets back at least what they put in before anyone holding ordinary shares gets a rupee. The standard Indian term is 1x non-participating, which means one times the money invested, and the investor must then choose between taking that preference or converting to ordinary shares and taking their percentage. They cannot have both.

body.context: TiffinBox must sell for more than its preference stack before the founders receive a single rupee. Every round you raise adds to this number, which is why a large raise at a high valuation is not a free lunch.

children.text: Read the last column downwards. The founders own 28.51% throughout, but they receive 0%, then 10.13%, then 21.39%, and only at ₹200 crore do they finally get the percentage they actually own. Above that point the preference stops mattering, because every investor is better off converting and taking their share.

body.title: What the founders receive: preference reality vs ownership arithmetic (₹ crore)

content.caption: Non-participating means choosing the better of the two, never both

children.text: Take the ₹60 crore exit. Series B first: converting would give 7,014 ÷ 35,071 × ₹60 crore = ₹12 crore, which is far below its ₹40 crore preference, so it takes the preference. That leaves ₹20 crore and 28,057 shares.

Series A next: converting would give 7,014 ÷ 28,057 × ₹20 crore = ₹5 crore, below its ₹6.25 crore preference, so it takes the preference too. That leaves ₹13.75 crore and 21,043 shares. Seed fund: converting gives 5,000 ÷ 21,043 × ₹13.75 crore = ₹3.27 crore, below its ₹4 crore preference, so it takes ₹4 crore. That leaves ₹9.75 crore and 16,043 shares.

The remaining ₹9.75 crore is shared by the ordinary holders: founders 10,000 shares get ₹6.08 crore, angels 1,250 get ₹0.76 crore, the note holder 584 gets ₹0.35 crore and option holders 4,209 get ₹2.56 crore. The founders' ₹6.08 crore is 10.13% of a ₹60 crore sale, against 28.51% ownership.

body.text: Three terms compound and any two of them together can change a founder outcome completely: a multiple above 1x, participation, and stacked seniority. A 2x participating preference on a large round means the investor is repaid twice their money and then still takes their full percentage of the rest. If you must concede one, concede seniority. Fight hardest against a multiple and against participation.

In India, these outcomes are usually delivered contractually rather than through an actual liquidation. On a share sale, the buyer's consideration is distributed among the sellers according to the waterfall agreed in the shareholders' agreement and reflected in the articles. A genuine winding-up is a different process altogether, where the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code priority applies and secured creditors, employee dues and other statutory claims are paid well before any shareholder. A liquidation preference decides how shareholders share what comes to shareholders, not what comes ahead of them.

body.title: Founders' proceeds at ₹100 crore
body.prompt: TiffinBox sells for ₹100 crore. The Series B takes its ₹40 crore preference, and everyone else converts and shares the remaining ₹60 crore across 28,057 shares. The founders hold 10,000 of those shares. How much do the founders receive, in ₹ crore, to two decimal places?
body.explanation: 10,000 ÷ 28,057 × ₹60 crore = ₹21.39 crore. That is 21.39% of the sale proceeds for a 28.51% stake. The Series B's ₹40 crore came off the top, and its own conversion value would only have been ₹20 crore, so it was better off taking the preference.

body.title: Name the structure
body.textWithBlank: A preference that pays the investor their money back first and then also lets them share the remaining proceeds pro rata is called a ___ preference.
body.explanation: Non-participating means the investor chooses between the preference and converting. Participating means they take both, which is why it is often called a double dip.

body.title: Which offer is better for you?
body.question: Your company has a ₹30 crore preference stack. Two acquirers bid. Bidder A offers ₹80 crore with the existing 1x non-participating preferences applying. Bidder B offers ₹95 crore, but as a condition the lead investor's preference is amended to 2x participating. You and your co-founder hold 30% of a company with 40,000 fully diluted shares, and the lead investor put in ₹20 crore for 10,000 shares. Which is better for the founders?
options: Bidder B, because ₹95 crore is a bigger number than ₹80 crore
Bidder A, because under B the lead takes ₹40 crore first and then still shares the remainder
They are identical once the preference stack is paid
Bidder B, because participation only applies to the lead investor
body.explanation: Under A, the ₹30 crore stack comes off ₹80 crore, leaving ₹50 crore, and the founders' 30% of the fully diluted company gives them about ₹15 crore, assuming the other preference holders convert. Under B, the lead takes 2x its ₹20 crore, which is ₹40 crore, plus the other ₹10 crore of preferences, leaving ₹45 crore, and it then also takes its 25% share of that remainder. The founders end up with roughly ₹13.5 crore. The bigger headline is worth less to you.

body.title: The offer that pays you nothing
body.scenario: You founded a Chennai logistics startup that has raised ₹72 crore across three rounds, all 1x non-participating and stacked, with the latest round being ₹50 crore. Growth has stalled. A strategic buyer offers ₹68 crore for the company. You and your co-founder hold 31% fully diluted. Your team holds vested options worth nothing at this price. The latest investor is pushing you to accept.
body.prompt: What is your position, and what would you negotiate before signing anything?
body.modelAnswer:
First, understand the outcome. The preference stack is ₹72 crore and the offer is ₹68 crore, so the entire consideration goes to preference holders, in stack order, and the last round does not even recover its ₹50 crore in full once the others are considered. Founders, angels and option holders receive nothing. Your 31% is worth zero at this price.

What to negotiate before signing:
1. A carve-out for the team. Ask the buyer and the preference holders to agree a management or employee carve-out, a fixed percentage of consideration ring-fenced for founders and option holders ahead of the waterfall. This is common practice precisely because a deal nobody on the operating team benefits from is a deal that fails during integration.
2. Retention packages. A buyer acquiring a logistics business needs the team. Cash retention bonuses, joining grants in the acquirer or an earn-out linked to post-acquisition performance are all outside the waterfall.
3. Test whether the deal must happen now. If the company can reach profitability or a better bid with more runway, the preference stack does not go away but you keep the option open. Understand what the investors' funds need, because a fund near the end of its life behaves differently from one with time.
4. Check who can actually force this. Look at the drag-along clause and the reserved matters list. If the investors can drag you into a sale, your leverage is commercial rather than legal, which makes the carve-out conversation the one that matters.
5. Learn the lesson for next time: every rupee raised at a high valuation adds to the stack, and the stack decides what a modest exit is worth to you.

body.title: Reading a preference term
steps: Note the multiple for every round, and add them up to get the total preference stack.
Check whether each preference is participating or non-participating.
Check the seniority: stacked by round, or pari passu across all rounds.
Check for any accruing dividend that increases the preference over time.
Calculate your break-even exit price, the point at which ordinary holders start receiving anything.
Calculate the exit price at which every preference holder would rather convert, since that is where your percentage finally becomes real.
Model your own proceeds at three exit prices: pessimistic, expected and good.
Make sure the waterfall in the shareholders' agreement is reflected in the articles of association.

cards.definition: The right of preference shareholders to be paid a defined amount out of exit proceeds before ordinary shareholders.
The investor receives either their money back once or their pro-rata share on conversion, whichever is higher, but not both.
The investor takes the preference amount and then also shares in the remaining proceeds.
The total of all liquidation preferences that must be satisfied before ordinary shareholders are paid.
A waterfall where later rounds are paid before earlier ones, rather than everyone sharing equally.
Preference holders rank equally and share proportionately if proceeds are insufficient.
A portion of exit proceeds ring-fenced for founders and employees ahead of the preference waterfall.
The exit price at which proceeds first exceed the preference stack and ordinary shareholders begin to receive money.

points: A liquidation preference pays investors before ordinary shareholders, so your percentage only decides how the remainder is split.
The Indian standard is 1x non-participating, where the investor picks the preference or conversion, not both.
TiffinBox's ₹50.25 crore preference stack means a sale below that price leaves the founders with nothing.
At ₹60 crore the founders receive ₹6.08 crore, which is 10.13% of proceeds for a 28.51% stake.
Only at ₹200 crore, where every investor prefers to convert, do the founders finally receive their full 28.51%.
Participation, multiples above 1x and stacked seniority compound. Fight hardest against multiples and participation.
Every round raised adds to the stack, so a large raise at a high valuation raises the bar your exit must clear.
If a modest exit is likely, negotiate a management carve-out and retention terms, which sit outside the waterfall.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not legal, tax or investment advice. TiffinBox Foods and the other companies and people described are fictional, and all amounts and percentages are illustrative. The waterfalls shown assume all options are exercised and ignore exercise proceeds, transaction costs, escrows, earn-outs and taxes, all of which change real outcomes. Actual entitlements depend on the terms of the shareholders' agreement and articles of association, and a genuine liquidation follows the statutory priority under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code rather than a contractual waterfall. Consult a qualified lawyer, company secretary or chartered accountant before relying on any exit calculation.
